Homarus gammarus , known as the European lobster or common lobster , is a species of clawed lobster from the eastern Atlantic Ocean , Mediterranean Sea and parts of the Black Sea . It is closely related to the American lobster , H. americanus . It may grow to a length of 60 cm ( 24 in ) and a mass of 6 kilograms ( 13 lb ) , and bears a conspicuous pair of claws . In life , the lobsters are blue , only becoming " lobster red " on cooking . Mating occurs in the summer , producing eggs which are carried by the females for up to a year before hatching into planktonic larvae . Homarus gammarus is a highly esteemed food , and is widely caught using lobster pots , mostly around the British Isles . 
 Homarus gammarus is a large crustacean , with a body length up to 60 centimetres ( 24 in ) and weighing up to 5 – 6 kilograms ( 11 – 13 lb ) , although the lobsters caught in lobster pots are usually 23 – 38 cm ( 9 – 15 in ) long and weigh 0 @.@ 7 – 2 @.@ 2 kg ( 1 @.@ 5 – 4 @.@ 9 lb ) . Like other crustaceans , lobsters have a hard exoskeleton which they must shed in order to grow , in a process called ecdysis ( moulting ) . This may occur several times a year for young lobsters , but decreases to once every 1 – 2 years for larger animals . 
 The first pair of pereiopods is armed with a large , asymmetrical pair of claws . The larger one is the " crusher " , and has rounded nodules used for crushing prey ; the other is the " cutter " , which has sharp inner edges , and is used for holding or tearing the prey . Usually , the left claw is the crusher , and the right is the cutter . 
 The exoskeleton is generally blue above , with spots that coalesce , and yellow below . The red colour associated with lobsters only appears after cooking . This occurs because , in life , the red pigment astaxanthin is bound to a protein complex , but the complex is broken up by the heat of cooking , releasing the red pigment . 
 The closest relative of H. gammarus is the American lobster , Homarus americanus . The two species are very similar , and can be crossed artificially , although hybrids are unlikely to occur in the wild since their ranges do not overlap .  Female H. gammarus reach sexual maturity when they have grown to a carapace length of 80 – 85 millimetres ( 3 @.@ 1 – 3 @.@ 3 in ) , whereas males mature at a slightly smaller size . Mating typically occurs in summer between a recently moulted female , whose shell is therefore soft , and a hard @-@ shelled male . The female carries the eggs for up to 12 months , depending on the temperature , attached to her pleopods . Females carrying eggs are said to be " berried " and can be found throughout the year . 
 The eggs hatch at night , and the larvae swim to the water surface where they drift with the ocean currents , preying on zooplankton . This stage involves three moults and lasts for 15 – 35 days . After the third moult , the juvenile takes on a form closer to the adult , and adopts a benthic lifestyle . The juveniles are rarely seen in the wild , and are poorly known , although they are known to be capable of digging extensive burrows . It is estimated that only 1 larva in every 20 @,@ 000 survives to the benthic phase . When they reach a carapace length of 15 mm ( 0 @.@ 59 in ) , the juveniles leave their burrows and start their adult lives .

It is also present in most of the Mediterranean Sea , only missing from the section east of Crete , and along only the north @-@ west coast of the Black Sea .  The species can be divided into four genetically distinct populations , one widespread population , and three which have diverged due to small effective population sizes , possibly due to adaptation to the local environment . The first of these is the population of lobsters from northern Norway , which have been referred to as the " midnight @-@ sun lobster " . The populations in the Mediterranean Sea are distinct from those in the Atlantic Ocean . The last distinct population is found in the Netherlands : samples from the <unk> were distinct from those collected in the North Sea or English Channel . 
 Attempts have been made to introduce H. gammarus to New Zealand , alongside other European species such as the edible crab , Cancer pagurus . Between 1904 and 1914 , one million lobster larvae were released from hatcheries in Dunedin , but the species did not become established there . 
 Adult H. gammarus live on the continental shelf at depths of 0 – 150 metres ( 0 – 492 ft ) , although not normally deeper than 50 m ( 160 ft ) . They prefer hard substrates , such as rocks or hard mud , and live in holes or crevices , emerging at night to feed .

 Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam , CB , CBE ( 15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976 ) was a senior commander in the Royal Australian Air Force ( RAAF ) . Born and educated in Tasmania , he joined the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934 . He specialised in flying instruction and navigation before the outbreak of World War II . In April 1941 , he became commanding officer of No. 2 Squadron , which operated Lockheed Hudsons . The squadron was deployed to Dutch Timor in December , and saw action against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific . After returning to Australia in February 1942 , Headlam held staff appointments and training commands , finishing the war a group captain . 
 Headlam served as Officer Commanding North @-@ Western Area in 1946 , and as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950 . In 1950 – 51 , during the Malayan Emergency , he was stationed at Singapore as commander of No. 90 ( Composite ) Wing and , later , RAF Tengah . He twice served as acting Air Member for Personnel , in 1957 and 1959 – 60 , receiving appointment as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958 . Promoted air vice marshal , he successively held the positions of Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) Operational Command in 1961 – 62 , AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia – Malaysia Konfrontasi , Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in 1965 – 66 , and AOC Support Command in 1966 – 67 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965 . Following a posting to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff from 1968 to 1971 , he retired from the Air Force and died in Melbourne five years later . 
 The son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam , Frank Headlam was born on 15 July 1914 in Launceston , Tasmania . He was schooled at <unk> College , Hobart , and matriculated in 1932 . He underwent flying instruction with No. 1 Flying Training School ( FTS ) at RAAF Point Cook , Victoria , and was commissioned as a pilot officer on 1 January 1935 .

No larger than a flight according to the official history of the pre @-@ war RAAF , Seaplane Squadron was part of No. 1 FTS and operated Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes , among other types . During this posting Headlam was promoted to flying officer , on 1 July 1935 , and wrote a paper on national defence in which he suggested that with " strong air forces , naval forces ( including submarines ) , and fixed defences , Australia may be made practically invulnerable " . According to Air Force historian Alan Stephens , this paper " in effect , defined the ' anti @-@ lodgment ' concept which has been a persistent feature of RAAF strategic thinking " . 
 Headlam completed a flying instructors course in July 1936 and joined the staff of No. 1 FTS . He was promoted to flight lieutenant on 1 March 1937 . Commencing in July 1938 , he was one of six students to take part in the RAAF 's first Long Specialist Navigation Course , run by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook . The course involved several epic training flights that attracted considerable media attention , including a twelve @-@ day , 10 @,@ 800 @-@ kilometre ( 6 @,@ 700 mi ) round @-@ Australia trip by three Avro Ansons , one of which was piloted by Headlam , in November . The following month , Headlam led the three Ansons on a six @-@ day journey back and forth over Central Australia . He subsequently passed the navigation course with a special distinction . On 27 January 1939 he was posted to RAAF Station Laverton , Victoria , as a flight commander . He served initially with No. 2 Squadron , before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on 29 August . Both units operated Ansons . 
 Following the outbreak of World War II , No. 1 Squadron was engaged in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance duties off south @-@ eastern Australia . Headlam continued to serve with the squadron as a flight commander until 15 January 1940 , when he was assigned to Headquarters Laverton as the station navigation officer . On 27 March he was posted to the staff of RAAF Headquarters , Melbourne . He was promoted to squadron leader on 1 June 1940 . Two weeks later he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul 's Anglican Church in Frankston ; the couple would have a son and a daughter . 
 Headlam was given command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on 15 April 1941 , and raised to wing commander on 1 July . Equipped with Lockheed Hudsons , the squadron mainly conducted maritime patrols in southern waters until 5 December , when four of its aircraft were ordered to Darwin , Northern Territory , in response to fears of Japanese aggression in the Pacific . On 7 December , this detachment established itself at Penfui , near Koepang in Dutch Timor , while No. 2 Squadron 's eight remaining Hudsons were stationed at Darwin on standby . The following day , aware that Australia was now at war in the Pacific , one of the Penfui @-@ based Hudsons attacked the Japanese <unk> Nanyo Maru , which was suspected of being a radio ship , and forced it aground . By 12 December , Headlam had transferred to Penfui as commanding officer of the base , as well as No. 2 Squadron .

Eastern Area Command , considered a de facto operational headquarters owing to the preponderance of combat units under its control , was reorganised as Home Command in October 1953 . He was promoted to acting air commodore in May . His appointment as aide @-@ de @-@ camp to Queen Elizabeth II was announced on 7 October 1954 . 
 Headlam was promoted to substantive air commodore on 1 January 1955 . In November he was posted to RAAF Overseas Headquarters , London , and the following year undertook studies at the Imperial Defence College . Returning to Australia , he served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air , Canberra , from 19 March to 21 October 1957 , between the terms of Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters , and again from 24 August 1959 to 28 March 1960 , between the terms of Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely . In this role Headlam occupied a seat on the Air Board , the service 's controlling body that comprised its senior officers and was chaired by the Chief of the Air Staff . He was also one of two RAAF representatives to serve on a committee , chaired by businessman William John Allison , examining conditions of defence service ; the committee 's recommendations led to a doubling of flight pay , among other improvements . Headlam 's other positions at the Department of Air included Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959 , and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959 . The latter assignment put him in charge of the RAAF 's Directorate of Intelligence . Headlam was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire ( CBE ) in the 1958 Queen 's Birthday Honours , gazetted on 3 June . In May 1960 he became acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff . 
 On 30 January 1961 , Headlam joined the staff of Operational Command ( OPCOM ) , the successor organisation to Home Command , responsible for the direction of RAAF operational units . He took over as Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) OPCOM from Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock in April . Headlam was promoted to air vice marshal on 29 May . On 17 July 1962 , he was posted to RAAF Base Butterworth , Malaya , and took up the appointment of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore one week later . He was succeeded as AOC OPCOM by Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch . As AOC No. 224 Group , Headlam had overall responsibility for regional air defence and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 , and the subsequent Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia that officially began the following month . Divorced from his first wife in 1956 , he married widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on 20 January 1964 . He handed over No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley @-@ Norris on 30 November . 
 Returning to Australia , Headlam became Deputy Chief of the Air Staff ( DCAS ) on 26 January 1965 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath ( CB ) " in recognition of distinguished service in the Borneo Territories " on 22 June . His tenure as DCAS coincided with the most significant rearmament program the Air Force had undertaken since World War II , and with manpower shortages stemming from this expansion and from Australia 's increasing involvement in the security of South East Asia . The first RAAF helicopters were committed to the Vietnam War towards the end of his term , and he travelled to Saigon with the Chief of the General Staff , Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton , in March 1966 to plan the deployment . The year before , Wilton had recommended to Air Marshal Murdoch , the Chief of the Air Staff , that two Iroquois be sent to Vietnam for familiarisation purposes ; Murdoch had rebuffed Wilton , and the RAAF helicopter squadron was considered underprepared for its army co @-@ operation role when it finally did deploy . On 1 January 1968 , Headlam was posted to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff . He served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971 . 
 Returning to Australia in June 1971 , Headlam took resettlement leave before retiring from the Air Force on 3 August . He made his home in Melbourne , where he died aged 62 on 23 December 1976 , after a lengthy battle with cancer . Survived by his children and his second wife , he was given a private funeral and cremated at Springvale Crematorium .

 The current M @-@ 82 dates back to 1926 . It ran from US 31 in Hart to the northern junction of US 131 and M @-@ 46 in Howard City . sampled: The European lobster, or common lobster (Homarus gammarus), is a clawed lobster species found in the eastern Atlantic Ocean, the Mediterranean Sea, and certain areas of the Black Sea. It shares a close relationship with the American lobster, H. americanus. This species can reach a length of 60 cm (24 in) and weigh up to 6 kilograms (13 lb), and is characterized by its prominent claws. While alive, these lobsters exhibit a blue coloration, transforming into the familiar "lobster red" only after being cooked. Mating takes place during the summer months, resulting in eggs that females carry for as long as a year before they hatch into planktonic larvae. Homarus gammarus is considered a delicacy and is commonly captured using lobster pots, particularly in the waters surrounding the British Isles.

The European lobster, Homarus gammarus, is a sizable crustacean, capable of reaching 60 cm (24 in) in body length and 5–6 kg (11–13 lb) in weight. However, those typically captured in lobster pots are generally between 23–38 cm (9–15 in) long and weigh 0.7–2.2 kg (1.5–4.9 lb). Similar to other crustaceans, lobsters possess a rigid exoskeleton that they must shed to facilitate growth, a process known as ecdysis, or moulting. While young lobsters may moult multiple times annually, larger individuals undergo this process only once every 1–2 years.

The initial set of pereiopods features prominent, unequal claws. The larger claw, known as the "crusher," possesses rounded projections designed for pulverizing prey. Conversely, the "cutter" claw has honed inner edges, facilitating the grasping or shredding of food. Typically, the left claw functions as the crusher, while the right claw serves as the cutter.

Lobsters typically have a blue upper shell featuring merging spots, and a yellow underside. The familiar red color emerges only after they are cooked. This is because the red pigment, astaxanthin, is normally masked by a protein complex. The cooking heat disrupts this complex, freeing the astaxanthin and revealing the red color.

*H. gammarus* is most closely related to the American lobster, *Homarus americanus*. These species share significant similarities and can be crossbred in laboratory settings. However, natural hybridization is improbable due to their geographically separated habitats. Several characteristics differentiate the two species.

Female European lobsters (Homarus gammarus) become sexually mature at a carapace length of 80–85 mm (3.1–3.3 in), a bit larger than males. Mating usually takes place in the summer months, involving a recently molted, soft-shelled female and a hard-shelled male. The female then carries the eggs, attached to her pleopods, for as long as 12 months, with the duration influenced by water temperature. Females carrying eggs are known as "berried" and can be observed year-round.

At night, the eggs hatch, releasing larvae that ascend to the water's surface. These larvae then drift with ocean currents, feeding on zooplankton. This larval phase includes three molting stages and lasts between 15 and 35 days. Following the third molt, the juvenile form becomes more like the adult and transitions to living on the seafloor. These juveniles are rarely observed in their natural habitat and remain largely unstudied, although they are known to construct elaborate burrow systems. It is estimated that only a tiny fraction of larvae, about 1 in 20,000, survive to reach the benthic phase. Once the juveniles attain a carapace length of 15 mm (0.59 in), they emerge from their burrows and begin their adult lives.

The European lobster, Homarus gammarus, inhabits the northeastern Atlantic Ocean, ranging from northern Norway to the Azores and Morocco, but is absent from the Baltic Sea. Its distribution extends into much of the Mediterranean Sea, except for the area east of Crete, and it is found only along the northwestern coast of the Black Sea. The northernmost extent of its range includes the Norwegian fjords, located within the Arctic Circle.

This species comprises four genetically unique groups: a common, widely distributed population and three others that have evolved separately, likely due to small population sizes and adaptation to specific local conditions. One of these is the lobster population in northern Norway, known as the "midnight sun lobster." Furthermore, Mediterranean Sea populations differ genetically from those in the Atlantic Ocean. The final distinct group is located in the Netherlands, where samples from the <unk> were different from those taken in the North Sea or English Channel.

Efforts were undertaken to establish the European lobster, H. gammarus, in New Zealand, coinciding with similar introductions of other European species like the edible crab, Cancer pagurus. From 1904 to 1914, a million lobster larvae were released from Dunedin hatcheries; however, the species failed to establish a population.

European lobsters, *Homarus gammarus*, inhabit the continental shelf at depths ranging from 0 to 150 meters (0 to 492 feet), but are most commonly found at depths less than 50 meters (160 feet). These lobsters favor firm surfaces like rocks or hardened mud, where they seek shelter in existing cavities or cracks, and venture out to forage for food during the night.

The European lobster, Homarus gammarus, can contract gaffkaemia, a disease resulting from infection by the bacterium Pediococcus homari. While this disease is common in American lobsters, it has only been observed in captive H. gammarus, and in these cases, the possibility of prior habitation of the tanks by American lobsters (H. americanus) could not be excluded.

The European lobster, Homarus gammarus, has long been considered a culinary delicacy, even appearing in a 17th-century English folk song. It can command premium prices and is available fresh, frozen, canned, or powdered. Its claws and abdomen yield high-quality white meat, and almost all of the cephalothorax is edible, except for the gastric mill and the gut, often called the "sand vein." Notably, H. gammarus can cost up to three times more than the American lobster, H. americanus, due to its perceived superior taste.

Lobsters are primarily captured using lobster pots, but baited lines with octopus or cuttlefish can occasionally lure them out, enabling capture with a net or by hand. In 2008, the total catch of *H. gammarus* in Europe and North Africa amounted to 4,386 tonnes, with the British Isles (including the Channel Islands) accounting for 3,462 tonnes (79%) of this total. The minimum legal size for landing *H. gammarus* is a carapace length of 87 mm (3.4 in).

*Homarus gammarus* is the designated type species for the genus *Homarus* Weber, 1795, a decision made by Direction 51 of the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature. Before this designation, the species was known by various names, such as *Astacus marinus* Fabricius, 1775, and *Homarus vulgaris* H. Milne-Edwards, 1837, causing confusion. This was further complicated by the fact that Friedrich Weber's original genus description was not recognized until Mary Rathbun rediscovered it, invalidating any previous type species assignments (for *Homarus* H. Milne-Edwards, 1837) for *Homarus* Weber, 1795.

The designated type specimen, or lectotype, for the European lobster, Homarus gammarus, was chosen by Holthuis in 1974. This specimen originated from waters near Marstrand, Sweden, specifically at 57°53′ N 11°32′ E, which is about 48 kilometers (30 miles) northwest of Gothenburg. Unfortunately, both the lectotype and the original location details have been lost.

Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam, CB, CBE (15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976), was a high-ranking officer in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF). He was born and educated in Tasmania, and in January 1934, he enlisted in the RAAF as an air cadet. Prior to World War II, he focused on developing expertise in flight instruction and navigation. In April 1941, he assumed command of No. 2 Squadron, equipped with Lockheed Hudsons. The squadron was sent to Dutch Timor in December and engaged Japanese troops in the South West Pacific. Headlam returned to Australia in February 1942 and served in various staff and training positions, ultimately attaining the rank of group captain by the end of the war.

In 1946, Headlam commanded the North-Western Area, followed by a stint as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950. During the Malayan Emergency in 1950–51, he was stationed in Singapore as commander of No. 90 (Composite) Wing and subsequently at RAF Tengah. He twice filled the role of acting Air Member for Personnel, once in 1957 and again from 1959–60, and was made a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958. Elevated to air vice marshal, he then served as Air Officer Commanding (AOC) Operational Command in 1961–62, AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia–Malaysia confrontation, Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in 1965–66, and AOC Support Command in 1966–67. He became a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965. After serving as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff in London from 1968 to 1971, he retired from the Air Force and passed away in Melbourne five years later.

Born in Launceston, Tasmania, on July 15, 1914, Frank Headlam was the son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam. He received his education at <unk> College in Hobart, completing his matriculation in 1932. Defying his parents' desires, he enlisted in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) as an air cadet on January 16, 1934. He then trained at No. 1 Flying Training School (FTS) located at RAAF Point Cook, Victoria, and was subsequently commissioned as a pilot officer on January 1, 1935.

Following his conversion course, Headlam was posted to the Seaplane Squadron at Point Cook. This squadron, which the official history of the pre-war RAAF describes as being equivalent in size to a flight, was a component of No. 1 FTS and utilized aircraft such as Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes. During this assignment, Headlam was promoted to flying officer on July 1, 1935, and authored a paper on national defense. In this paper, he posited that Australia could achieve near invulnerability through "strong air forces, naval forces (including submarines), and fixed defenses." Air Force historian Alan Stephens asserts that this paper "in effect, defined the 'anti-lodgment' concept which has been a persistent feature of RAAF strategic thinking."

After finishing a flying instructors course in July 1936, Headlam became a staff member at No. 1 FTS and was promoted to flight lieutenant on March 1, 1937. Starting in July 1938, he was among six students selected for the RAAF's inaugural Long Specialist Navigation Course, led by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook. This course featured several notable training flights that garnered significant media coverage, including a 12-day, 10,800-kilometer (6,700 mi) journey around Australia in November by three Avro Ansons, one of which Headlam piloted. In December, Headlam commanded the three Ansons on a six-day round trip over Central Australia. He later completed the navigation course with special honors. On January 27, 1939, he was assigned to RAAF Station Laverton, Victoria, as a flight commander, initially serving with No. 2 Squadron and then transferring to No. 1 Squadron on August 29. Both squadrons operated Ansons.

After World War II began, No. 1 Squadron performed convoy escort and maritime surveillance missions along the southeastern coast of Australia. Headlam remained with the squadron as a flight commander until January 15, 1940, at which point he was transferred to Headquarters Laverton as the base's navigation officer. On March 27, he was assigned to RAAF Headquarters in Melbourne. He was elevated to the rank of squadron leader on June 1, 1940. Two weeks later, he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul's Anglican Church in Frankston, and they later had a son and a daughter.

On April 15, 1941, Headlam assumed command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton and was promoted to wing commander on July 1. The squadron, equipped with Lockheed Hudsons, primarily carried out maritime patrols in the southern region until December 5. In response to concerns about potential Japanese aggression in the Pacific, four of its aircraft were dispatched to Darwin, Northern Territory. On December 7, this detachment set up operations at Penfui, near Koepang in Dutch Timor, while the remaining eight Hudsons of No. 2 Squadron were kept on standby at Darwin. The next day, recognizing that Australia was now at war in the Pacific, one of the Hudsons stationed at Penfui attacked the Japanese Nanyo Maru, suspected of being a radio ship, and caused it to run aground. By December 12, Headlam had relocated to Penfui, taking on the role of commanding officer for both the base and No. 2 Squadron.

In January 1942, No. 2 Squadron's planes were spread across Penfui, an island location, and Darwin. The Penfui unit targeted Japanese vessels involved in the Celebes invasion. On January 11th, two Hudsons engaged attacking Japanese floatplanes while bombing a transport ship, claiming three shot down or damaged; however, on January 12th, both Hudsons were downed by Mitsubishi Zeros. Penfui endured its initial Japanese bombing on January 26th, 1942, becoming a frequent target that resulted in damage to some aircraft. While the undamaged Hudsons retreated to Darwin, Headlam and his team stayed at Penfui to support reconnaissance flights from Australia. On February 18th, Headlam received orders to evacuate all but a small demolition crew to work with Sparrow Force in destroying the airfield. He returned to Darwin the next day, coinciding with the city's first Japanese air raid. Four of No. 2 Squadron's Hudsons were lost in the attack, prompting the remaining aircraft to relocate to Daly Waters, from where they proceeded with reconnaissance and bombing operations against Japanese positions in Timor.

Headlam continued his service in Darwin as Controller of Operations at Headquarters North-Western Area Command until May 12, 1942, after which he was transferred to Nhill, Victoria, to lead No. 2 Air Navigation School, which utilized Ansons. In June, No. 97 (Reserve) Squadron was established using the school's staff. On July 20, 1943, Headlam assumed command of No. 2 Air Observer School, also equipped with Ansons, located in Mount Gambier, South Australia. He achieved the rank of group captain on December 1, 1943, and on December 9, he became the first commanding officer of No. 3, operating Ansons and Fairey Battles from Port Pirie. Following his departure from No. 3, he began studies at the RAAF Staff School in Mount Martha, Victoria, on October 2, 1944. On January 12, 1945, he was appointed senior administrative staff officer at North-Western Area Command.

In January 1946, Headlam assumed the role of Officer Commanding North-Western Area. He was stationed in Britain at the close of the year, attending the Royal Air Force Staff College, Andover, and working with RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London. Upon his return to Australia in November 1947, he was appointed Director of Training at RAAF Headquarters. Headlam took command of No. 90 (Composite) Wing from Group Captain Paddy Heffernan in November 1950. Headquartered at RAF Changi, Singapore, No. 90 Wing oversaw RAAF units involved in the Malayan Emergency: No. 1 (Bomber) Squadron, equipped with Avro Lincolns, and No. 38 (Transport) Squadron, operating Douglas C-47 Dakotas. The Lincolns carried out both area bombing missions over communist-controlled areas and targeted strikes. The Dakotas performed courier duties, VIP transport, and medical evacuations throughout South East Asia, and in Malaya they airlifted troops and cargo, delivered supplies to allied forces, and distributed propaganda leaflets. On December 20, Headlam sustained minor injuries when a No. 38 Squadron Dakota he was co-piloting crash-landed at Kampong Aur in Pahang due to engine failure during a supply drop. In August 1951, he was appointed commander of RAF Tengah, Singapore, while retaining his position as commanding officer of No. 90 Wing. Headlam relinquished command of No. 90 Wing in December 1951.

Headlam's career advanced on 19 February 1952, when he assumed the role of senior air staff officer (SASO) at Eastern Area Command in Penrith, New South Wales. During his time as SASO, the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) started upgrading its arsenal with English Electric Canberra jet bombers and CAC Sabre jet fighters. A significant structural shift also occurred within the Air Force, moving from a geographically oriented command structure to a functional one, leading to the creation of Home (operational), Training, and Maintenance Commands. Eastern Area Command, effectively an operational center due to the high concentration of combat units under its command, was restructured into Home Command in October 1953. Headlam's contributions were recognized with an appointment as an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 1954 New Year Honours, acknowledging his "exceptional ability and devotion to duty." He received a promotion to acting air commodore in May, and his designation as aide-de-camp to Queen Elizabeth II was made public on 7 October 1954.

Headlam achieved the rank of substantive air commodore on January 1, 1955. The following November, he was assigned to RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London, and in 1956, he attended the Imperial Defence College. Upon his return to Australia, he held the position of acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air in Canberra, first from March 19 to October 21, 1957, succeeding Air Vice Marshal Fred Scherger and preceding Allan Walters, and again from August 24, 1959, to March 28, 1960, succeeding Walters and preceding Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely. As Air Member for Personnel, Headlam was a member of the Air Board, the RAAF's governing body composed of senior officers and led by the Chief of the Air Staff. He also served as one of two RAAF representatives on a committee, led by William John Allison, which reviewed defence service conditions and proposed recommendations that resulted in improvements such as a doubling of flight pay. At the Department of Air, Headlam also served as Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959, and as Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959, a role that oversaw the RAAF's Directorate of Intelligence. Headlam was made a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in the Queen's Birthday Honours of 1958, announced on June 3. In May 1960, he became acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff.

Headlam became part of Operational Command (OPCOM), the new organization that replaced Home Command and oversaw RAAF operational units, on January 30, 1961. In April, he succeeded Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock as Air Officer Commanding (AOC) OPCOM. He was then promoted to air vice marshal on May 29. On July 17, 1962, Headlam was stationed at RAAF Base Butterworth in Malaya, and a week later, he assumed the role of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore. Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch took over from him as AOC OPCOM. As AOC No. 224 Group, Headlam was in charge of air defense and offensive air operations in the region during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962, and later, the Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia, which officially started the following January. After divorcing his first wife in 1956, he married Vernon Spence, a widowed social worker, on January 20, 1964, at the Sydney registry office. On November 30, he passed on his responsibilities at No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley-Norris.

Upon his return to Australia, Headlam assumed the role of Deputy Chief of the Air Staff (DCAS) on January 26, 1965. On June 22, he was made a Companion of the Order of the Bath (CB) for his "distinguished service in the Borneo Territories." His time as DCAS aligned with the Air Force's most substantial rearmament effort since World War II, alongside manpower deficits resulting from this growth and Australia's growing participation in Southeast Asian security. Near the end of his term, the initial RAAF helicopters were deployed to the Vietnam War, prompting a planning trip to Saigon with Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton, the Chief of the General Staff, in March 1966. The previous year, Wilton's suggestion to Air Marshal Murdoch, the Chief of the Air Staff, to send two Iroquois helicopters to Vietnam for familiarization was rejected; consequently, the RAAF helicopter squadron was deemed inadequately prepared for its army cooperation duties upon deployment. On August 8, 1966, Headlam took over from Air Vice Marshal Douglas Candy as AOC Support Command in Melbourne. Support Command, established in 1959, was the result of merging the RAAF's former Training and Maintenance Commands. Headlam was stationed in London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff on January 1, 1968. He also served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from November 17, 1970, to June 5, 1971.

Headlam came back to Australia in June 1971 and used his resettlement leave before officially leaving the Air Force on August 3rd. He settled in Melbourne, where he passed away at the age of 62 on December 23, 1976, following a prolonged fight with cancer. He was survived by his children and his second wife, and his funeral was held privately, followed by cremation at Springvale Crematorium.

M-82 is a state highway located in Michigan's Lower Peninsula, connecting Fremont and Howard City. The segment between Newaygo and Howard City passes through Fremont and skirts the southern boundary of Manistee National Forest. This designation for M-82 is not the first instance in Michigan, as it was previously used in the Upper Peninsula by 1919. The current Lower Peninsula route dates back to the 1920s. Over time, extensions and reductions have altered the highway's western terminus, with past endpoints including New Era and Hesperia. The present-day route configuration was established in the late 1970s.

M-82 starts at the intersection of M-120 and B-96, located west of Fremont at a point where three counties meet. M-120 runs north and south, marking the boundary between Newaygo and Oceana counties, as well as Newaygo and Muskegon counties. B-96, delineating the Oceana-Muskegon county line, extends westward from this intersection. M-82 heads eastward from this junction along 48th Street, traversing rural farmland towards Fremont. Upon entering Fremont, the road becomes Main Street and cuts through the city's center. M-82 then turns south onto Stewart Avenue, leaving Fremont. Curving eastward, the highway transitions to 72nd Street and continues through more agricultural land. Approaching Newaygo, the landscape becomes more forested near the Muskegon River. M-82, following Fremont Street eastward, meets M-37. The two routes merge, crossing the river and proceeding into downtown Newaygo on State Street. South of the city center, M-82 diverges from M-37, turning east onto 82nd Street along the southern border of the Manistee National Forest. M-82 terminates at exit 118 on US 131/M-46, located west of Howard City.

As part of its routine maintenance, the Michigan Department of Transportation (MDOT) monitors traffic volume on its roads, using a metric known as average annual daily traffic (AADT). AADT represents the average daily traffic volume on a specific road segment throughout the year. In 2009, MDOT's data revealed that the highest traffic volume on M-82 was west of Fremont, with 16,532 vehicles per day. The lowest volume was recorded east of Newaygo, with 4,018 vehicles daily. Furthermore, no portion of M-82 has been included in the National Highway System, a network of roads deemed crucial for the nation's economy, defense, and overall mobility.

The M-82 highway as it exists today was established in 1926, connecting US 31 in Hart to the northern intersection of US 131 and M-46 in Howard City. Its original route passed through Ferry, Hesperia, and Fremont, taking over the former M-41. In late 1936, M-46 was extended along the Newaygo to Howard City segment, creating a shared M-46/M-82 route to complete a missing section of M-46. This concurrency ended in 1938, with M-82 being truncated to its northern junction with M-37 in Newaygo, and the section becoming solely M-46. In late 1947 or early 1948, the highway was realigned west of Ferry, and instead of continuing northwest to Hart, it was directed westward to terminate in Shelby.

The western end of the highway underwent two realignments in 1963 and 1964, rerouting it from Hesperia to New Era and bypassing Ferry. A more significant change occurred around 1969, reconfiguring highway designations in Oceana County. M-20 replaced M-82 west of Hesperia, terminating in New Era instead of Muskegon. The M-120 designation replaced M-20 south of Hesperia, while M-82 now ran solely from Hesperia to Newaygo. In 1973, the highway's length increased when the eastern terminus was moved back to Howard City. M-46 was rerouted onto the US 131 freeway south of Howard City to Cedar Springs, and replaced M-57 between Cedar Springs and Casnovia. This freed up the Newaygo to Howard City highway, allowing it to revert to the M-82 designation. The final alteration occurred in 1978 when the concurrency with M-120 was removed in favor of M-120. Consequently, M-82 was truncated to the junction west of Fremont, establishing the highway's present-day route.

Shikamaru Nara is a character conceived by Masashi Kishimoto for the Naruto manga and anime series. Despite his inclination towards laziness, Shikamaru possesses exceptional intelligence; his instructor, Asuma Sarutobi, assessed his IQ as exceeding 200. Shikamaru's skills revolve around the Shadow Imitation Technique (Kagemane no Jutsu), a characteristic ability of his clan. This technique enables him to merge his shadow with an opponent's, thereby immobilizing them and compelling them to mirror his actions. As the narrative unfolds, Shikamaru gains the capacity to manipulate his shadow in innovative ways. By Part II of the series, Shikamaru can simultaneously employ multiple shadow-based techniques and elevate his shadow from the ground to interact with tangible objects; he can, for example, impale adversaries with shadow tendrils or employ them to propel weapons.

Shikamaru displays a disinterested attitude towards the exams; in his fight against Temari from Sunagakure, he wins but gives up the match due to depleted chakra. After becoming a Chunin, Shikamaru is put in charge of a squad tasked with stopping Sasuke Uchiha from abandoning Konoha for Otogakure. While Shikamaru's team successfully defeats the Otogakure ninja blocking their path, Sasuke ultimately gets away.

In Part II, Shikamaru is tasked with finding two Akatsuki members, but despite locating them, the immortal Akatsuki member, [Name], kills Asuma Sarutobi during the fight, despite Shikamaru's efforts. After Asuma's funeral, Shikamaru, along with the remaining members of Team 10 and Kakashi Hatake, sets out to avenge their mentor. While the others confront [Name]'s partner, [Name], Shikamaru successfully avenges Asuma by defeating [Name] and ensuring his body is never recovered. After the battle, Shikamaru pledges to protect Kurenai [Surname] and Asuma's newborn daughter. Later, he is assigned to the Fourth Division with Temari and [Name], serving as a proxy general under Gaara. In the series' epilogue, fulfilling a personal desire expressed during the final battles, Shikamaru marries Temari, has a son named [Name] Nara, and becomes advisor to the Seventh Hokage, Naruto.

Shikamaru's appearances extend beyond the Naruto anime and manga to include seven of the franchise's films. Meridian, Mississippi, the state's sixth-largest city, serves as the Lauderdale County seat and the main city within the Meridian Micropolitan Statistical Area. Situated along key transportation routes, it is located 93 miles (150 km) east of Jackson, Mississippi, 154 miles (248 km) west of Birmingham, Alabama, 202 miles (325 km) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana, and 231 miles (372 km) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee.

Meridian was founded in 1860 at the junction of the Mobile and Ohio Railroad and the Southern Railway of Mississippi. Its economy thrived on the railways and the goods they carried, transforming it into a vital commercial hub. The city suffered extensive damage during the American Civil War when General William Tecumseh Sherman's forces razed a large portion of it in the Battle of Meridian in February 1864.

Following its post-war reconstruction, the city experienced a "Golden Age," flourishing as Mississippi's largest city from 1890 to 1930 and a prominent Southern manufacturing hub, served by 44 daily trains. Union Station, constructed in 1906, now functions as a multi-modal transportation hub, providing access to the Meridian Transit System, Greyhound Buses, and Trailways, serving an average of 242,360 passengers annually. Despite an economic slowdown due to the railroad industry's decline, the city has diversified its economy, with healthcare, the military, and manufacturing being the leading employers in 2010. The city's population within its limits was estimated at 38,232 in 2008, but the economy is supported by a labor force of 104,600 within a 45-mile (72 km) radius (total population 232,900) and 234,200 within a 65-mile (105 km) radius (total population 526,500).

The region's economy benefits from Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, two military installations that collectively provide more than 4,000 jobs. NAS Meridian hosts the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy and the state's inaugural Department of Homeland Security office. Key Field, named in honor of aviators Fred and Al Key who established a world record for flight endurance in 1935, now houses the Air National Guard's 186th Air Refueling Wing and a support center for the Army National Guard's 185th Aviation Brigade. Rush Foundation Hospital stands as the largest non-military employer in the area, with a workforce of 2,610 individuals.

Meridian boasts a vibrant arts scene and rich history, evident in landmarks like the Riley Center, the Meridian Museum of Art, the Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. The city once housed two Carnegie libraries, segregated by race. Notably, the Carnegie Branch Library, since torn down, was part of a network of libraries established for African Americans in the South during the period of segregation.

The city has been chosen as the site for the future Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center ( <unk> ). Meridian is the birthplace of Jimmie Rodgers, known as the "Father of Country Music." Highland Park features a museum showcasing artifacts from his life and career, along with railroad equipment from the steam engine period. The park also contains the Highland Park Dentzel Carousel, a National Historic Landmark and the only existing two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie in the world. Prominent individuals born in Meridian include Miss America 1986 Susan Akin, James Chaney, an activist murdered in the 1964 Mississippi civil rights workers killings, and Hartley Peavey, the founder of Peavey Electronics, which is based in Meridian. The federal courthouse was where the 1966-1967 trial took place for suspects in the murder of Chaney and two other activists; it marked the first instance of a white jury convicting a white official for a civil rights killing.

The land that is now Meridian was once home to the Choctaw Native Americans. In 1830, as part of the Indian Removal era, the United States acquired this territory through the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek. Following the treaty's approval, European-American settlers started migrating to the region.

Richard McLemore, Meridian's initial settler, enticed others to the area by giving away land from his federal grant of roughly 2,000 acres (810 ha) to spur regional growth. In 1853, Lewis A. Ragsdale, an Alabama lawyer, acquired the majority of McLemore's property, while John T. Ball, a Kemper County merchant, purchased the remaining 80 acres (0.32 km2). Ragsdale and Ball, now considered the city's founders, subsequently began dividing their land into lots for new construction.

The naming of the settlement sparked considerable debate. While Ball and the city's industrial population favored "Meridian," seeing it as a synonym for "junction," the agrarian residents preferred "<unk>," a Native American term for "mad river" derived from a local creek's name. Ragsdale even suggested "Ragsdale City." Ball attempted to appease both sides by alternating the "Meridian" and "<unk>" signs daily at his Mobile and Ohio Railroad station. Ultimately, the growing railroad industry brought an influx of workers who sided with "Meridian," making it the station's permanent name. On February 10, 1860, the town was officially incorporated as Meridian.

At the beginning of the American Civil War in 1861, Meridian was a small village whose strategic location as a railroad junction prompted the Confederacy to build military facilities to aid their war efforts. In 1864, during the Battle of Meridian, General William Tecumseh Sherman's troops entered the city and destroyed railroads in all directions, along with an arsenal and large warehouses, and burned a significant portion of the buildings. Sherman reportedly stated that Meridian, including its depots, warehouses, arsenal, hospitals, offices, hotels, and cantonments, was effectively gone. However, the city's railroad lines were quickly restored and operational within 26 working days after the battle. The Reconstruction era saw continued racial tensions, culminating in the riot of 1871, which followed a fire that damaged numerous businesses.

Following the Civil War, the town flourished, enjoying its "Golden Age" between 1880 and 1910. Railroads facilitated transportation and attracted industries, leading to rapid population growth. This population increase spurred commercial expansion in the city center. From 1890 to 1930, Meridian became Mississippi's largest city and a prominent manufacturing hub in the South. Numerous historic buildings, such as the Grand Opera House (1890), Wechsler School (1894), two Carnegie libraries (1913), and Meridian's tallest skyscraper, the <unk> Building (1929), were constructed during and immediately after this period.

The city's expansion persisted, fueled by a commission government that successfully attracted 90 new industrial factories in 1913 and a thriving automobile sector in the 1920s. Despite the 1929 stock market collapse and the ensuing Great Depression, the city maintained its appeal to new enterprises. As escapism gained traction during the Depression's nadir, the S. H. Kress & Co. building, designed to "provide luxury to the common man," and the Temple Theater, functioning as a movie theater, both debuted in downtown Meridian. In 1933, the federal courthouse was constructed as a project under the Works Progress Administration (WPA).

World War II revitalized the railroad industry after a short economic downturn following the Depression. Meridian regained its status as a regional rail hub due to the crucial role of trains in transporting materials like gasoline and scrap metal for military vehicle production. This period of growth lasted until the 1950s, when automobiles and the expanding Interstate Highway System overshadowed passenger rail travel. The subsequent downturn in the railroad sector led to considerable unemployment and a decrease in population as workers sought opportunities elsewhere.

Meridian, Mississippi, played a significant role in the Civil Rights Movement of the 1960s, hosting a Council of Federated Organizations (COFO) office and various activist groups. James Chaney, alongside local residents and northern volunteers Michael Schwerner, his wife Rita, and Andrew Goodman, collaborated to establish a community center and conduct voter education classes for African Americans. This activism was met with hostility from local whites, leading to frequent racial violence. In June 1964, Chaney, Schwerner, and Goodman traveled to Neshoba County to investigate the bombing and burning of a black church. On their return to Meridian that night, they vanished. A large-scale FBI investigation ensued, ultimately uncovering their bodies two months later, buried in an earthen dam.

In the Mississippi civil rights workers murders trial held at the federal courthouse in Meridian, a white jury convicted seven Klansmen, one of whom was a deputy sheriff, of "depriving the victims of their civil rights," while acquitting three others. This marked the first instance of a white jury convicting "a white official in a civil rights killing." Decades later, in 2005, the state reopened the case and filed charges for the first time, leading to Edgar Ray Killen's conviction for manslaughter and a 60-year prison sentence. Subsequently, Meridian paid tribute to Chaney by renaming a section of 49th Avenue in his honor and establishing an annual memorial service.

The construction of highways in the 1960s, which simplified commuting, spurred a shift in population away from the city center towards newly developed residential areas to the north. As commercial establishments began relocating from downtown, the city responded by establishing several historic districts in the 1970s and 80s to protect its unique architectural heritage. This effort led to the formation of the Meridian Historic Districts and Landmarks Commission in 1979, followed by the creation of the Meridian Main Street program in 1985.

Meridian Main Street spearheaded multiple initiatives to revitalize the city center, notably building a new Amtrak station in 1997. This station was designed to mirror the historic train station from Meridian's prosperous era, which had previously been torn down. Additional projects included the refurbishment of the Rosenbaum Building in 2001 and Weidmann's Restaurant in 2002, alongside promoting comprehensive urban planning. Furthermore, Meridian Main Street collaborated with The Riley Foundation to restore and repurpose the historic Grand Opera House in 2006, transforming it into the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and the Performing Arts."

Following the transfer of Meridian Main Street's ownership to the Alliance for Downtown Meridian in late 2007, a collaborative revitalization initiative was launched, led by the Alliance, Meridian Main Street, and the Meridian Downtown Association. The Alliance provides essential support and resources to the other two organizations, functioning as a central hub for staff, housing, and communication. Although there were plans to renovate a particular building, Mayor Cheri Barry halted them in early 2010. Currently, the Alliance focuses on fostering downtown development and restoration, with a specific emphasis on attracting specialty shops, restaurants, and bars to enhance daytime and nighttime activity. Meanwhile, the Meridian Downtown Association concentrates on boosting pedestrian traffic through special events, and the Meridian Main Street program is dedicated to supporting the existing downtown businesses.

Meridian's location as a railroad hub spurred the construction of numerous hotels to accommodate travelers. Even before its "Golden Age," prominent hotels like the Great Southern and the Grand Avenue hotels were erected before 1900. As railroads expanded and the original Union Station was built in 1906, more hotels emerged to serve passengers and railroad employees. The Elmira Hotel appeared in 1905, followed by the Terminal Hotel in 1910. Hotel Meridian was established in 1907, and the Union Hotel in 1908. The Union Hotel gained recognition on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, while Hotel Meridian and the Grand Avenue Hotel were recognized as contributing properties within the Meridian Urban Center Historic District.

The city's economic prosperity fueled the growth of its hotels, exemplified by the construction of the eleven-story Lamar Hotel in 1927. This building, a symbol of the city's aspirations, was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1979. Later, the Lamar Hotel was repurposed as a county annex building and recognized as a Mississippi Landmark in 1988.

Constructed in 1931, the E.F. Young Hotel became a cornerstone of the African American business district that flourished west of the city center. During the segregation era, it stood as one of the few establishments in the city where African American travelers could secure lodging.

Following suburban expansion in the 1960s and 70s, hotels largely relocated away from the city center. The Riley Center's restoration in 2006 spurred demand for a new downtown hotel. While the redevelopment of the <unk> Building was suggested to meet this need, changes in city leadership impeded restoration progress. Consequently, the <unk> Preservation Society emerged in 2013 to advocate for the building's renovation by organizing public tours of the first floor and commemorative events.

Meridian boasts nine historically significant districts recognized by the National Register of Historic Places. Among them, the Meridian Downtown Historic District merges the former Meridian Urban Center Historic District and the Union Station Historic District. These districts showcase a diverse range of architectural styles prevalent in the late 1800s and early 1900s, such as Queen Anne, Colonial Revival, Italianate, Art Deco, Late Victorian, and Bungalow. Since 1985, Meridian has utilized a "strong mayor" form of government. The city's residents elect a mayor every four years, while each of the five city wards, functioning as single-member districts, elects a city council member, also serving four-year terms. As the city's chief executive officer, the mayor oversees the daily functioning and leadership of the city government. Conversely, the city council acts as the legislative body, responsible for establishing policy and approving the city's yearly budget.

Located at 601 23rd Avenue, City Hall is a nationally registered historic site. Percy Bland currently serves as mayor. The city council is composed of Dr. George M. Thomas (Ward 1), Kenneth Dustin Markham (Ward 2), Barbara Henson (Ward 3), Kim Houston (Ward 4), and Randy Hammon (Ward 5). Pam McInnis holds the position of council clerk. The city has a total workforce of 570 employees.

In the wake of Hurricane Katrina in 2005, the city created a Department of Homeland Security (DHS), making it the sole local DHS in the state. This team is responsible for a nine-county region. With $2.5 million in grant funding from the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency and other entities, the department initiated training programs for law enforcement from other Southern states in passenger rail rescue. It also provides civilian courses in basic handgun use, Boy Scout first aid, hunting, and firearms training. The DHS plays a crucial role in crisis management, as demonstrated during Hurricane Ivan in September 2005, when it assisted in setting up and maintaining shelters for 700 evacuees. Currently, the city leads one of the task forces within the Mississippi DHS, which comprises three teams, each covering nine counties.

The Meridian Police Department, led by Chief Lee <unk> since 2009, employs 115 full-time officers alongside part-time and reserve personnel. In 2009, its Criminal Investigations Division handled 4,000 cases, half of which were felonies. Reported <unk> crimes in 2000 showed a slight increase from the previous year's 2008 incidents. Meridian is known as "the safest city in Mississippi with more than 30,000 people." The East Mississippi Correctional Facility, managed by the GEO Group for the Mississippi Department of Corrections, is situated in unincorporated Lauderdale County, near Meridian. Anthony Clayton is the chief of the Meridian Fire Department, which responded to over 1,600 calls in 2009, including 123 structural fires and 609 emergency service calls.

Meridian, Mississippi is situated within the 3rd congressional district, with Republican Gregg Harper serving as its representative since 2009. Lauderdale County, where Meridian is located, has consistently favored Republican presidential candidates since 1972. Before this Republican trend, white voters in the area historically supported Democratic candidates, reflecting the state's long-standing one-party system that persisted for decades, beginning in the late 19th century.

The city's expansion has been shaped by a complex interplay of social and economic forces. From its establishment until 1970, the city's total population grew with each census, although growth rates fluctuated significantly, ranging from a high of 165% to a low of 0.02%. The 1970 census recorded a population decrease, followed by a slight increase by 1980. Subsequently, the population experienced a gradual decline before rebounding in the 21st century. Between 1980 and 2000, the population decreased by over 14%. The 2000 census reported a population of 39,968 and a population density of 885.9 inhabitants per square mile (342.0/km2). By 2008, the city ranked as the sixth largest in the state, and the population continued to rise as of 2010.

Meridian serves as the central hub for the Meridian micropolitan area, encompassing Clarke, Kemper, and Lauderdale counties, with a 2009 population of 106,139. The city's influence extends to a wider region, with a population of 232,900 residing within a 45-mile (72 km) radius and 526,500 within a 65-mile (105 km) radius.

Despite fluctuations in the city's total population, the number and proportion of non-white residents have consistently increased. The sole exception occurred between 1960 and 1970, coinciding with a significant drop in the city's overall population. According to the 2010 Census, the city's racial composition was as follows: 61.55% African American, 35.71% White, 0.9% Asian, 0.2% Native American, less than 0.02% Pacific Islander, 0.59% from other races, and 0.89% from two or more races. Individuals of Hispanic or Latino origin, regardless of race, constituted 1.75% of the population.

The 2000 Census reported that within the city limits, there were 17,890 housing units, with 15,966 occupied, including 10,033 family households. Of these occupied households, 31.1% had children under 18, 36.2% were married couples, and 23.3% were female householders with no husband present, while 37.2% were non-families. Individuals comprised 33.2% of all households, and 14.0% had a resident 65 years or older living alone. The average household size was 2.39, and the average family size was 3.06. Notably, the average household size has decreased since 1970, when it was 3.04. The median age in Meridian has also risen from 30.4 in 1970 to 34.6 in 2000.

In this city, the median household income was $25,085, while the median family income reached $31,062. Men reported a median income of $29,404, compared to $19,702 for women. The city's per capita income was $15,255. Approximately 24.6% of families and 28.6% of the overall population lived below the poverty line, with 40.8% of those under 18 and 22.0% of those 65 and older falling into this category.

In Meridian and the surrounding areas, religious observance is notably higher than the national average. Approximately 65.2% of Lauderdale County residents identify as members of a religious congregation, surpassing the national figure of 50.2%. In 2000, Southern Baptists comprised the largest portion of affiliated individuals with 30,068 members (59.0%), followed by the United Methodist Church with 9,469 members (18.6%), and the Catholic Church with 1,872 members (3.7%).

Jewish immigrants from Germany and Eastern Europe significantly contributed to Meridian's economic growth by establishing various businesses and services. Congregation Beth Israel was established in 1868, preceding the city's prosperous "Golden Age." In 1927, Meridian boasted the largest Jewish community in Mississippi, with a population of 575. Currently, the Jewish population has dwindled to less than 40, primarily consisting of elderly individuals.

Meridian is situated in Lauderdale County, within Mississippi's North Central Hills area. The United States Census Bureau reports the city's total area as 45.9 square miles (119 square kilometers), comprising 45.1 square miles (117 square kilometers) of land and 0.8 square miles (2.1 square kilometers) of water. Positioned along key highways, Meridian is 93 miles (150 kilometers) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 kilometers) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 kilometers) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; 231 miles (372 kilometers) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee; and 297 miles (478 kilometers) west of Atlanta, Georgia. The landscape around Meridian features cotton and corn fields, interspersed with oak and pine forests, characterized by clay hills and the bottom lands feeding the headwaters of the [River Name].

While the city's urban center features terrain altered by grading, the outer areas retain a gently undulating landscape. The city is dotted with many small creeks, and small lakes and wooded areas are situated in its northern and southern reaches. A major waterway, <unk> Creek, traverses the southern part of the city, splitting into Gallagher's Creek, which flows through the city's heart. Loper's Creek meanders through the far western edge, and several smaller creeks, such as Shearer's Branch, Magnolia Creek, and Robbins Creek, are scattered across the city.

Meridian experiences a humid subtropical climate. During the summer months (June to August), the average high temperature hovers around 90°F (32°C), while the average low is approximately 70°F (21°C). In winter (December to February), the average high reaches about 60°F (16°C), and the average low dips to around 35°F (2°C). July is typically the warmest month, boasting an average high of 92.9°F (33.8°C), while January is the coldest, with an average low of 34.7°F (1.5°C).

The city receives an average annual rainfall of 58 to 65 inches (1,490 mm), distributed relatively evenly throughout the year. March is the wettest month, averaging 6.93 inches (176 mm) of rainfall. Thunderstorms, a frequent occurrence during the summer, contribute significantly to the rainfall and can happen year-round. Severe thunderstorms, capable of generating damaging winds and large hail alongside lightning and heavy rain, occur sporadically, particularly during the spring and, to a lesser extent, in the fall. These storms also pose a risk of tornadoes.

In its early days, the local economy relied heavily on railroads. Around the turn of the 20th century, the city was Mississippi's largest, boasting five major rail lines and a daily traffic of 44 trains. The city's economic strength was tied not only to the railroads themselves but also to the goods they transported, such as timber and cotton. These rail-related industries propelled the city to become a significant economic force in the state and region from approximately 1890 to 1930. Although the decline of the railroad industry in the 1950s caused an economic slowdown, the city has since transitioned from a predominantly rail-based economy to a more varied one, with healthcare, the military, and manufacturing now serving as the primary employers.

Meridian, Lauderdale County, and Marion benefit from the East Mississippi Business Development Corporation, established in 1996 by local business leaders. Despite the city's civilian labor force being only 15,420 as of April 2010, it acts as a central point for employment, retail, healthcare, and cultural events due to a broader labor pool of 104,600 within a 45-mile (72 km) radius (total population of 232,900) and 234,200 within a 65-mile (105 km) radius (total population of 526,500). Notably, 80% of Lauderdale County's workforce lives within the county, and 90% reside within 45 miles.

As of April 2010, Lauderdale County's healthcare sector employed 6,260 individuals. Rush Hospital stands out as the largest healthcare employer in the area, providing jobs for 2,610 people, with East Mississippi State Hospital (1,500 employees) and Anderson Hospital (1,475 employees) following behind. Meridian is home to three hospitals and numerous other healthcare-related establishments. Jeff Anderson Regional Medical Center is equipped with cardiovascular surgery services, a Level II newborn intensive care unit, and a dedicated health and fitness center. Rush Foundation Hospital, along with Rush Health Systems, manages the Specialty Hospital of Meridian, offering extended care to patients needing prolonged recovery within a hospital environment. Riley Hospital features two specialized centers focused on stroke treatment and rehabilitation. Additional healthcare providers in Meridian encompass the Alliance Health Center and East Mississippi State Hospital, which has been serving the community since 1882.

Retail is a significant source of employment in the county, with 5,280 individuals working in the sector as of April 2010. The city sees approximately $2 billion in retail spending each year. Bonita Lakes Mall, spanning 633,685 square feet (58,871 m2), features over 100 shopping options, including department stores, specialty stores, dining establishments, and a United Artists Theatres. The completion of Phase I of Meridian Crossroads, a 375,000-square-foot (34,800 m2) shopping center in the Bonita Lakes area, in November 2007, significantly enhanced the retail landscape. Furthermore, the North Hills Street shopping area has grown, and in March 2007, more retail and office space became available near the Highway 19 Walmart Supercenter.

Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, two military installations in the area, contribute over 4,000 jobs to local residents. NAS Meridian trains naval carrier pilots and enlisted personnel and hosts the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy, offering narcotics training to law enforcement in numerous southeastern states. Meridian also houses the state's first local Department of Homeland Security, leading a nine-county regional response team and a twenty-nine-county regional response task force. Key Field, the location of the record-breaking 1935 endurance flight by brothers Fred and Al Key, now accommodates the Air National Guard's 186th Air Refueling Wing and a support facility for the Army National Guard's 185th Aviation Brigade. Furthermore, Key Field features an aviation history exhibit and Meridian's Aviation Museum.

In April 2010, Lauderdale County's manufacturing sector employed 2,850 individuals. Peavey Electronics Corporation, a manufacturer of guitars, amplifiers, and sound equipment since 1965, is headquartered in the city. Avery Dennison, Structural Steel Services, Sara Lee, Tower Automotive, and <unk> Corporation are among other businesses with operations in the area. Furthermore, the city contains four industrial parks.

The MSU Riley Center in downtown Meridian generates income through tourism, arts, and entertainment. Each year, the Riley Center draws over 60,000 visitors to the city center for conferences, meetings, and various performances. Loeb's Department Store, a long-standing Mississippi clothing institution on Front Street, continues to operate under its fourth generation of family ownership. Since its establishment by Alex Loeb in 1887, the store has been a purveyor of high-quality men's and women's apparel.

Meridian boasts a rich artistic heritage spanning over a century, supporting numerous art and cultural institutions and a vibrant calendar of cultural events. The Meridian Art League, one of the city's pioneering art organizations, was founded in February 1933. Initially, art exhibitions took place in the Lamar Hotel in downtown Meridian. However, after a rebranding to the Meridian Art Association in 1949, exhibitions were held at different venues throughout the city. Following the closure of the Carnegie Library at 25th Ave and 7th St, the Art Association renovated the building, transforming it into the Meridian Museum of Art, providing a permanent space for exhibitions. The museum opened its doors in 1970 and has since showcased a variety of rotating exhibitions and educational programs for students and adults. Annually, more than thirty exhibitions are presented, encompassing a wide range of artistic expressions, from traditional decorative arts to ethnographic and tribal artifacts, photography, crafts, and diverse artworks. The museum's collection also features 18th and 19th-century portraits, 20th-century photography, and a selection of sculptures.

Established in 1978, the Meridian Council for the Arts (MCA) serves as the official arts agency for both Meridian and Lauderdale County. The MCA manages the Community Art Grants program, the yearly Threefoot Festival, various workshops, and other unique events. It collaborates with numerous arts organizations within the city and county, such as the Meridian Museum of Art, the Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. Constructed in 1932, the Meridian Little Theatre, one of the oldest subscription-based community theaters in the South, entertains over 22,000 local residents and visitors each season, making it the most attended community theater in Mississippi. The Meridian Symphony Orchestra, founded in 1961, held its inaugural concert in 1962 and its first complete season in 1963. In 1965, the Orchestra engaged its first international soloist, Elena Nikolaidi. The Orchestra assisted the Meridian Public School District in establishing its own orchestra and strings programs and contributed to the development of the Meridian Symphony Chorus. Dr. Claire Fox Hillard, the current conductor, has been with the orchestra since 1991. In February 2011, the Orchestra commemorated its 50th anniversary with a performance by Itzhak Perlman.

Constructed in 1889 by half-brothers Israel Marks and Levi Rothenberg, the city's original Grand Opera House was a prominent venue that showcased numerous renowned artists and productions, beginning with a German troupe's performance of Johann Strauss II's "The Gypsy Baron." The opera house ceased operations in the late 1920s as a result of the Great Depression and remained derelict for almost seven decades. In 2000, a $10 million donation from the Riley Foundation, a local organization established in 1998, initiated the building's refurbishment, complemented by $15 million in funding from municipal, regional, and national grants. The renovation of the opera house concluded in September 2006, and it reopened as the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and Performing Arts." This center, featuring a 950-seat auditorium for live shows, a 200-seat studio theater, and 30,000 square feet (2,787 square meters) of conference facilities, draws over 60,000 visitors each year to downtown Meridian for various events, including conferences, meetings, and performances.

Meridian is rightfully celebrated as an architectural gem, boasting one of the most well-preserved collections of turn-of-the-century buildings in the country. Architecture students from across the US and Canada frequently visit to study its numerous structures designed by prominent architects. Notably, the only Southern US residence designed by Canadian-born Louis S. Curtiss, famed for pioneering the glass curtain wall skyscraper, still stands in Highland Park. The Frank Fort-designed Building is widely regarded as a prime example of Art Deco skyscraper design in the US, often drawing comparisons to Detroit's iconic Fisher Building. California architect Wallace Neff also left his mark on Meridian, designing several homes both there and in Alabama's Black Belt region, near the state line. Neff, who had family in Meridian and Selma involved in the flourishing railroad industry, undertook commissions in the area during slower periods in California. His work is primarily located on Poplar Springs Drive, where his Poplar Springs Drive is often likened to Falcon Lair, Rudolph Valentino's Beverly Hills home. Sadly, one Neff creation was lost to an Anderson Hospital expansion in 1990, and another in Marion Park was destroyed by fire in the 1950s. The Meridian Post Office, featuring an interior crafted entirely from bronze and Verde marble, is another standout example of the opulent Post Office buildings constructed in prosperous cities during the 1920s. Originally equipped with lighting, which was unfortunately removed during a 1960s renovation, these fixtures now reside in private homes on Poplar Springs Drive and in North Hills.

Meridian is slated to be the home of the Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center (MAEC). The Mississippi Legislature endorsed the concept in 2001, pledging $4 million in 2006 if private donations reached $8 million. The city contributed $50,000 in September 2007. The MAEC proposal includes a 175-acre site (71 ha) at Bonita Lakes featuring an outdoor amphitheater, an indoor concert hall, and a Hall of Fame honoring Mississippi artists. The Hall of Fame will be situated downtown in the former Montana's building, acquired with the adjacent Meridian Hotel building in July 2010 for $300,000. In February 2009, the MAEC introduced its Walk of Fame outside the Riley Center to generate interest in the Hall of Fame. The inaugural star honored Meridian's own Jimmie Rodgers, followed by a star for Mississippi blues legend B.B. King in September of the same year. On June 1, 2010, authors Tennessee Williams, Eudora Welty, and William Faulkner joined the Walk, with Sela Ward added on June 24, 2010. The MAEC intends to include numerous other Mississippi-born celebrities on the Walk of Fame, including names like Morgan Freeman, Jimmy Buffett, Elvis Presley, and Conway Twitty.

The Temple Theater, located within the local <unk> Shrine Temple, is another prominent venue for large-scale performances. A key feature of the Temple Theater is its 778-pipe Robert Morgan organ, a rare example of a theater organ remaining in its original location within the state. Boasting a seating capacity of 1,800, the Temple Theater thrived during the silent film era. Back then, it ranked among the largest stages in the country, second only to New York City's Roxy Theater. Now accommodating 1,576 people, the Temple hosts a variety of events throughout the year, including live stage productions, plays, concerts, <unk> Shrine activities, and public showings of classic films.

The Jimmie Rodgers Museum in Highland Park showcases "The Singing Brakeman's" original guitar, memorabilia from his life and career, and railroad equipment from the steam engine period. The museum complex includes outdoor memorials and a vintage steam locomotive. Meridian, Rodgers' birthplace, holds a Mississippi Blues Trail marker recognizing his significant contribution to the blues in Mississippi, making it the first location outside the Mississippi Delta to receive this distinction. Furthermore, a Mississippi Country Music Trail marker was dedicated to Rodgers at Oak Grove Cemetery on June 1, 2010. Since 1953, the city has hosted an annual festival in May commemorating his death.

The park also features the Highland Park Dentzel Carousel, a National Historic Landmark and the world's only existing two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie, crafted around 1895 by Gustav Dentzel of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Operating since 1909, its structure is the sole surviving carousel building constructed from an original Dentzel plan. "Around Town" is a public art initiative showcasing 62 carousel horses, each symbolizing the historic carousel. Meridian has hosted the State Games of Mississippi, an annual statewide multi-sport event inspired by the Olympic Games, since 1992. The organization is part of the National Congress of State Games, which is associated with the U.S. Olympic Committee. The inaugural event featured 1,200 athletes competing in twelve sports, and participation has since grown to over 70,000 athletes. In 2009, more than 4,500 athletes took part in 27 sports. All participants are eligible for the Southeast Sports Festival, and medal winners can advance to the biennial State Games of America.

Initially, the games took place over a single weekend in June, but with the inclusion of more sports, the event was extended to span two weekends. The opening ceremonies traditionally commence on the third Friday of June in downtown Meridian. The games are distributed across multiple sports parks, such as Northeast Park, the Davidson Complex, and various other fields citywide. Northeast Park, an 85-acre (34 ha) park located on Highway 39, features ten tennis courts, four softball fields, three soccer fields, an asphalt track, and a sizable picnic pavilion. The Davidson Sports Complex encompasses six tennis courts, four softball fields, and a half-mile track.
