Meridian Regional Airport, situated at Key Field on Airport Boulevard South, provides air service to the city. It is located 3 miles (4.8 km) southwest of the city center. The airport boasts the longest public runway in Mississippi, measuring 10,004 feet (3,049 m). Operating since 1930, the airport provides daily flights to Dallas/Fort Worth, TX.

Amid the Great Depression, the city considered closing the airport due to upkeep expenses. However, in 1935, airport managers Fred and Al Key devised a plan to save it. The brothers flew their plane, the "Ole Miss," continuously over the city from June 4 to July 1, 1935. Their 27-day flight, lasting 653 hours and 34 minutes, garnered sufficient attention and financial support to keep the airport open. Consequently, the airport, named Key Field in their honor, recognizes the Key brothers, whose flight endurance record remains unmatched in traditional aviation.

Meridian's early public education system was established following the 1870 Mississippi Constitution. Between 1870 and 1885, the City Council appointed trustees to the Board of School Directors, which oversaw school operations. Prior to 1884, the city's schools were privately run, serving only around 400 students. Meridian's first publicly owned school was not constructed until September 1884. The initial public school for African American students operated in rented space at St. Paul Methodist Church. In January 1888, a change to the city charter by the Mississippi Legislature enabled Meridian to manage its own municipal school district. Subsequently, in March of that year, voters approved $30,000 in bonds for new public school construction. The Wechsler School, built in 1894 using these funds, became Mississippi's first brick public school building specifically for black students.

The Meridian Public School District started with a small area and expanded over time to its present configuration of six elementary schools, three middle schools, and three high schools. In addition to the public schools, the city also has private educational options like Lamar School, Calvary Christian School, Community Christian School, and St. Patrick's Catholic School. Meridian High School, the district's primary high school, is situated on a 37-acre (15 ha) campus with six buildings containing 111 classrooms, serving roughly 1,500 students in grades 10-12.

Meridian boasts two institutions of higher learning. Meridian Community College, established in 1937 at 910 Highway 19 N, provides free tuition for four semesters to graduates of Meridian Public and Lauderdale County School Districts, as well as homeschooled students within Lauderdale County. Initially named Meridian Junior College and situated at Meridian High School, the college relocated in 1965. Following desegregation, it merged with T.J. Harris Junior College, formerly serving African-American students, in 1970. In 1987, the institution was renamed Meridian Community College "to more accurately reflect the diversity of opportunities it provides for a growing community area." Mississippi State University also maintains a campus in Meridian. In the Fall of 2008, 763 students from 33 Mississippi counties and several Alabama counties were enrolled at the college.

Meridian is home to the Meridian @-@ Lauderdale County Public Library, situated at the intersection of 7th Street and 26th Avenue. The city once boasted two Carnegie libraries, both erected in 1913, serving the black and white communities separately. The Fortnightly Book and Magazine Club, established in the 1880s by a group of women, spearheaded the effort to build a library for Meridian, with their collection forming the initial basis of the library's holdings. Garnering widespread support, the club enlisted city leader Israel Marks to solicit funding from Andrew Carnegie. The library for blacks was constructed at 13th Street and 28th Avenue on land donated by St. Paul Methodist Church, while the library for whites was housed in a building acquired from the First Presbyterian Church of Meridian in 1911. Notably, the African American library was the sole library for blacks in Mississippi until after World War I and the only Carnegie library in the nation built specifically for African Americans. In 1967, in response to the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the two libraries integrated, merging their collections and relocating to their present site. The former white library was repurposed as the Meridian Museum of Art in 1970, while the original African American library was torn down on May 28, 2008.

Papa Stour, an island in the Shetland archipelago of Scotland, has a small population of fewer than twenty inhabitants, some of whom arrived following a recruitment initiative in the 1970s. Situated west of mainland Shetland and encompassing 828 hectares (3.2 square miles), it ranks as the eighth largest island in Shetland. The island's coastline is sculpted by the erosion of its fragile volcanic rock, resulting in a remarkable assortment of caves, sea stacks, arches, blowholes, and cliffs. Papa Stour and its adjacent waters are home to a wide array of wildlife. The island's western coast is designated as a Site of Special Scientific Interest, while the surrounding marine environment is recognized as a Special Area of Conservation.

The island features multiple Neolithic burial chambers and the ruins of Duke Hakon's 13th-century residence, a relic of Norse settlement. Its population peaked at over 380 in the 1800s, spurred by the establishment of a fishing station at <unk> in West Voe. Afterward, the population steadily decreased, but has since rebounded from a nadir of 16 in the 1970s.

Papa Stour lies off the southwestern tip of St Magnus Bay, boasting a dramatic, 34-kilometer (21-mile) coastline marked by many small inlets and four significant voes (bays). Housa Voe (from Old Norse, meaning "harbor bay") in the south offers the best protection for boats, and its adjacent cliffs feature a naturally formed rock arch. West Voe (from Old Norse, meaning "house bay") on the east side, while more exposed, serves as the island's primary harbor and the ferry terminal.

Holm and Maiden Stack flank the southern entrance to the harbor. Holm, a tidal island, served as a leper colony until the 18th century, though some believe many residents suffered from vitamin deficiencies instead of leprosy. Maiden Stack's name originates from a 14th-century tale. Lord Thorvald, according to legend, built a small house on its summit, the ruins of which remain, to shield his daughter from male attention. However, his plan failed when she became pregnant after leaving; another version claims she and her fisherman lover eloped successfully. Notably, peat is almost entirely absent, and the volcanic rock composition contributes to relatively fertile soils. The scarcity of peat resulted in turf scalping for fuel, exposing bare rock areas in the island's interior.

On June 21, 2008, Stuart Hill, the sole inhabitant and proprietor of the 2.5-acre island of Forvik Holm (which he calls "Forvik Island"), proclaimed its independence, establishing the Crown Dependency of Forvik. Citing a marriage agreement from 1468 between Norway's King Christian and Scotland's King James III, Hill asserted that the island should be a British crown dependency, separate from both the United Kingdom and the European Union. The island's geology features diverse volcanic and sedimentary rocks dating back to the Devonian period. During this era, Scotland was part of the Old Red Sandstone Continent, located between 10 and 25 degrees south of the equator. The Old Red Sandstone deposits, formed between 408 and 370 million years ago, resulted from the erosion of older Silurian rocks, uplifted during Pangaea's formation, and their subsequent deposition into river deltas. The freshwater Lake Orcadie extended along the edges of these eroding mountains, spanning from Shetland to the southern Moray Firth. Papa Stour's composition primarily consists of volcanic ash and lavas from this period's volcanic activity, including solidified layers of volcanic ash and rhyolite lava, alongside a Devonian fish bed at Lamba Banks. Numerous large boulders were also left behind by Pleistocene glaciation.

The sea's erosion of the island's soft volcanic rock has sculpted a remarkable assortment of caves, stacks, arches, blowholes, cliffs, voes, and other formations, considered some of the most impressive in Britain. The 'Holl o' is a cave that cuts directly through the island's northwest tip, stretching nearly half a mile in length and being broad enough for rowing. Papa Stour's waters and surrounding areas are often visited by otters, grey seals, killer whales, and harbour porpoises. The island is a breeding ground for various bird species, including Atlantic puffins, Arctic and common terns, and Arctic skuas, as well as northern fulmars, common guillemots, razorbills, curlews, wheatears, ringed plovers, and great black-backed gulls. Additionally, many migratory bird species have been observed on the island.

The island boasts a rich array of wildflowers, such as mountain everlasting, spring squill, and an unidentified species, alongside the common heather. The western coast holds the designation of a Site of Special Scientific Interest, while the waters surrounding Papa Stour are recognized as a Special Area of Conservation. Furthermore, the native Shetland Pony continues to be bred on the island.

The island's history of human habitation extends back to around 3000 BC, evidenced by the remnants of Neolithic burial sites identified as "heel-shaped cairns." While information about the pre-Celtic and Celtic periods remains scarce, it is believed that the Norse discovered a religious community upon their arrival. The island's name originates from <unk> <unk>, signifying "Big island of the Papar" (Celtic monks), differentiating it from Papa Little, located approximately 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) westward.

Papa Stour is featured in a 1299 Old Norse manuscript, Shetland's oldest existing document. It recounts a dramatic event that occurred in the home of Duke Hakon Magnusson, who later became King Hakon V of Norway. Near <unk> Voe beach, a stone circle marks the site of a 'ting,' or local assembly. The ruins of Duke Hakon's 13th-century residence are still visible near <unk> Voe.

While Shetland formally fell under Scottish rule in 1469, Norwegian landowners maintained their Papa Stour holdings until the 17th century. During the 1500s, merchants from Bremen and Hamburg established seasonal trading posts to purchase fish from local fishermen. By the 1700s, the island was owned by two Scottish landowners, Thomas Gifford of Busta and Arthur Nicolson of Lerwick. They oversaw a successful haaf (Old Norse for 'deep sea') fishing operation, conducted during the summer using sixareen boats.

Established in 1806, the island church commands a view of Kirk Sand in Fore Wick Bay. Approximately 300 meters away, situated on the headland separating the western edge of Kirk Sand and an adjacent bay, possibly lies the location of a more ancient chapel. Locally known as the "blank kirk" and identified by the Ordnance Survey as "the site of a blank chapel dating back to around the twelfth century," it is said that supernatural forces disrupted construction at this earlier site, undoing each day's progress overnight. Legend has it that these otherworldly entities relocated the cornerstones to the church's current location, enabling successful construction to proceed. Archaeological digs in 2004 unearthed primarily large rhyolite blocks and a fragment of whalebone rib, potentially lending credence to the local folklore.

During the 1800s, West Voe established a fishing station, leading to a population boom on the island, reaching at least 360 residents. However, from the 1870s onward, fuel scarcity and a decrease in fish stocks, caused by the arrival of steam drifters, triggered a population decline. Around this time, Papa Stour witnessed another peculiar incident: Edwin Lindsay, an Indian army officer and son of the 6th Earl of Balcarres, was deemed mentally unstable and banished to the island in disgrace for refusing to participate in a duel. He remained confined for 26 years until Catherine Watson, a Quaker preacher, secured his freedom in 1835. Lindsay's Well, a spring in the southern part of the island, marks the spot where he was permitted to take baths.

Horizontal water mills, also called Norse or Clack Mills, were common near Dutch Loch. These structures typically had two stories, turf roofs, and were built into hillsides for access to the upper level where the millstone was located. Inside, a stationary lower millstone and a rotating upper millstone were present, the latter powered by water impacting paddles beneath. Some of these mills remained operational on Papa Stour until the early 1900s, and a functional example still exists on the Burn of [location], at [location] in southern Mainland Shetland.

Like many small Scottish islands, Papa Stour's population reached its highest point in the 1800s, followed by a substantial decrease (similar to Mingulay). The island's school shut down by 1970, and the number of inhabitants dwindled to sixteen "fairly elderly" individuals. However, an advertisement in Exchange and Mart, offering a free croft and five sheep to newcomers, reversed this trend, attracting numerous applications. The 1981 census showed a population of 33. Unfortunately, internal conflicts and subsequent legal battles caused the population to drop to 20 by 2005, leading to departures and the school's closure. By early 2008, only nine people remained after a family of seven moved away. The 2011 census recorded 15 permanent residents, while overall Scottish island populations increased by 4% to 103,702 during the decade from 2001 to 2011.

On the evening of March 28, 1930, the Aberdeen trawler Ben Doran ran aground on the Ve Skerries, located 3 miles northwest of Papa Stour, while en route to Scalloway to unload its catch. Although the weather was initially favorable, the wreck was not discovered and reported by a passing trawler until the next day. By the time the coastguard and local volunteers (since Shetland had no lifeboat at the time) initiated rescue operations, the weather had worsened, making it impossible to reach the skerries. A request was made for the Stromness lifeboat from Orkney, only 120 miles away, but it was too late to be effective. Tragically, all nine crew members died in the shipwreck. Only three bodies were recovered: James Mitchell, who was returned to Aberdeen, and J. Cormack and J.R. <unk>, who were buried in Scalloway.

In February 1940, the SS Highcliffe cargo ship was shipwrecked on <unk> Holm due to heavy fog. Fortunately, the weather was favorable, and only the ship and its cargo were lost. Later, in 1967, the Aberdeen trawler Juniper ran aground in Lyra Sound, situated at the base of 60-meter (200-foot) cliffs. The <unk> lifeboat crew successfully rescued all 12 crew members, and the coxswain was awarded the RNLI silver medal for his bravery during the operation.

The most recent shipwreck off Papa Stour took place on December 9, 1977, when the Aberdeen-based trawler Elinor Viking, captained by Alec Flett, ran aground on the Ve Skerries. While the local lifeboat responded, severe sea conditions prevented it from approaching close enough to rescue the crew. Alec Webster, the Coastguard Station Officer in Lerwick, requested assistance, and a volunteer crew from Sumburgh Airport was dispatched in a British Airways Sikorsky helicopter. Despite gale-force winds, they successfully winched all crew members to safety within hours of the grounding. The helicopter crew was later recognized with bravery awards for their efforts. This incident, which resulted in no fatalities, led to the construction of a lighthouse on the skerries in 1979 and may have also spurred the establishment of the current Search and Rescue helicopter unit at Sumburgh Airport.

Crofting remains central to the island's way of life. A post office is located at the pier, but there is no shop. Mains electricity was only introduced to the island near the end of the 20th century. "Angel of Death," the first song on Slayer's 1986 album Reign in Blood, was penned by guitarist Jeff Hanneman. Both the lyrics and music center on Josef Mengele, a Nazi doctor who performed human experiments at Auschwitz during World War II. This song has been a source of controversy for Slayer, leading to enduring accusations of Nazi sympathies and racism.

Despite the controversy it stirred and its role in delaying the release of Reign in Blood, "Angel of Death" remains a staple in Slayer's live performances, appearing on all their live albums and DVDs, and has been included in various films. Critics have praised the song, with AllMusic's Steve Huey calling it a "classic."

While on tour, Slayer guitarist Jeff Hanneman came across books about Josef Mengele, a Nazi physician, which inspired him to write "Angel of Death." Hanneman recalled purchasing the books and thinking, "This has gotta be some sick shit." He explained that the lyrics for "Angel of Death" stemmed from the disturbing content he had read about Mengele, which remained in his mind when the band started working on their record.

The song's lyrics describe the surgical experiments Josef Mengele performed on inmates at the Auschwitz concentration camp during World War II. Mengele's research focused on groups like dwarfs and twins, involving both physical and psychological evaluations. "Angel of Death" specifically references experiments such as live experimental surgeries without anesthesia, blood transfusions between twins, isolation tolerance tests, gassing, lethal germ injections, sex change operations, organ and limb removals, and <unk>.

The lyric "joining heads...rip yourselves apart," taken from near the end of the song, alludes to the accusation that Josef Mengele surgically conjoined twins, resulting in one being deformed. This claim, describing how "the hunchback was sewn to the other child, back to back," with "their wrists back to back too," originated with Auschwitz survivor Vera Alexander during the 1961 trial of Adolf Eichmann, the "architect of the Holocaust." Alexander testified that Mengele "sewed the veins together," effectively creating "Siamese twins." This allegation gained broader recognition after Alexander appeared in the 1985 documentary *The Search for Mengele*, a film referenced by various writers, including Mengele expert Gerald Posner.

The controversial lyrics in "Angel of Death" were a factor in the delayed release of Slayer's 1986 album, Reign in Blood. Def Jam Records, the band's label, had their distributor, Columbia Records, decline to release the album because of the lyrical themes and concerns over the graphic nature of the artwork. Reign in Blood was ultimately released on October 7, 1986, by Geffen Records. However, the controversy surrounding the album meant it was not included in Geffen Records' official release schedule.
